231.t: Leo Feist and being told to stay away from New York offices
231.s: They sing and play two hours at the Leo Feist music publisher, whose manager tells them not to return to the manager's office.
231.q: So we go to the house, open up the trunk, take out our roller skates -- but I didn't tell you, this fella when we got to New York -- forgot to tell you that the man took us the next day down to Leo Feist, the biggest music publisher in New York City. He took us to Leo Feist on 7th Avenue between…

231.t: Roller skating across Broadway to Leo Feist
231.s: They skate to Feist's, hanging onto streetcars and crossing the third rail, drawing a crowd.
231.q: onto the car, we get up to 47th Street, between 47th and -- now, we're going to Leo Feist that's what I told you before -- we're going up there for the first time since we were first there to tell them what has happened -- the manager of the music publishers and tell him what had happened.

126.t: Hearing a New Orleans-style band at Rector's in New York
126.s: On a weekend pass before going overseas, he and other soldiers heard a band playing the New Orleans tunes they loved.
126.q: Yes. And during the First World War, when I, before I went overseas in the First World War, we had heard that there was a tremendous New Orleans jazz band at Rising Webbers in New York. That's on 8th Avenue, just south of Columbus Circle. And, uh, on one, uh, weekend pass, about eight or ten of the…

22.t: Schiller Cafe to Reisenweber's: the New York sensation
22.s: The band gets the name Original Dixieland Jazz Band, goes to New York in January 1917 and becomes a hit at the 400 Room.
22.q: Over the Shilly cafe was made June. I mean March April and May And in June We work at the lab it could be in July It worked there to the last last part of December with shields This is the band that got the name original Dixieland jazz band Because prior to that we had no building We were building…

602.t: Big Apple jam sessions and playing with T. Gordon
602.s: Late-night jams at New York's Big Apple drew Stuff Smith, Eddie South and Harry James, and Gabriel toured army camps with a Teagarden-like trombonist.
602.q: Yeah. Yeah, I've seen quite a few of them. I never saw any of these women around New Orleans do that, but around New York, Chicago, they could do it. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But, uh. We used to have some sessions, as I started to tell you about that, that's how I run into Stuff Smith, they used to be in…

314.t: First day in New York and meeting Bill Evans at the Vanguard
314.s: In 1962 he meets Evans through Gene Lees and gets a front-row seat at the Village Vanguard.
314.q: Well Columbia brought us here and my first gig was at the Village Vanguard for a week. But actually that was after we’d been here a couple of weeks. My first day in New York, in ’62, it was in September I think, Gene Lees, who was the editor at Down Beat and he was a good friend and he was a…

536.t: First night in New York and 52nd Street
536.s: Brown arrives in New York at eighteen, stays with his aunt, and goes with his cousin to 52nd Street to see Byas, Billie Holiday, Tatum and Hawkins.
536.ch: Childhood and arrival in New York
536.q: Hell of a story. I’d like to have a dollar for every time I had to tell this story because I could go on a vacation for a long time.

439.t: First night at Small's and seeing Omer Avital
439.s: Her first visit to Small's in New York, seeing Omer Avital play, and an all-night hang before the bus back to Boston.
439.q: Wow that’s a beautiful question because you really brought me back to that moment. I mean the name of the club is called Small’s, which still exists, so I didn’t know what it was. I didn’t know at that time when I stepped into Small’s it was a new club that was encouraging young people to find who…

466.t: First days in New York: Junior's Bar and loft sessions
466.s: He went to Junior's Bar on 52nd Street, was taken to a jam session and met bassist Jack Six; the loft sessions were about camaraderie and learning.
466.q: Yeah. The first day I was there I went to Junior’s Bar. It was on 52nd Street between Broadway and Eighth Avenue. And someone told me, probably Bob Newman, as soon as

324.t: New York, Birdland and the Major Bowes contest
324.s: Gibbs says New York accepted him royally; he was house bandleader at Birdland six months a year and on the road the rest. He won Major Bowes at thirteen and jokes about hotel cockroaches.
324.q: I’m a hero. I grew up in New York and it’s very fortunate, I really did well in New York. I was accepted royally. I was the house band leader at Birdland in my younger days. There would always be Count Basie, Sarah Vaughan, Terry Gibbs, Duke Ellington, Dinah Washington, Terry Gibbs. But I was there…

519.t: The neo-soul wave of the late 1990s
519.s: He arrived in New York in 1997, worked with Bilal at Electric Lady, watched D'Angelo make Voodoo and gave Common piano lessons.
519.ch: Black Radio and the new waves
519.q: Well I think there was two waves of it. I think there was one wave in the early or late 90s, the neo-soul movement. I was in New York when that happened. I didn’t realize it at the time but it was happening. I got to New York in ’97. I met Bilal in ’97. We started working with his album. And we…

212.t: Arriving in New York and the first jam session
212.s: With no tuba on arrival he got one and went to a jam session with Roland Kirk, Carla and Paul Bley. Low expectations for tuba.
212.ch: Arriving in New York and Mingus
212.q: I had to find out what I had to find out. I didn’t want to be denied the opportunity just cause I didn’t show up. So there was no question of am I going to make it or, I just had to do what I had to do which was place myself in the right place. I didn’t have a tuba when I came to New York. I…

793.t: The New York scene in 1987: bebop and the young lions
793.s: When she arrived bebop was king; she played with the Twelve Tone Funk Orchestra, and teachers saw Wynton Marsalis as jazz police.
793.ch: Changes in the New York scene
793.q: Well the New York scene, I mean there are a lot of different scenes. So you know there’s the free scene, and if you’re just talking about jazz okay, but then there are all the other things like salsa and everything, but in jazz there’s the free scene and I played with this group called the Twelve…

501.t: Lower Manhattan arts scene and Ornette's Lonely Woman
501.s: How he learned jazz terminology in 1960s lower Manhattan among artists; Ornette played him Lonely Woman. Roommate painter Bob Thompson, pick-up basketball and bars with poets and painters.
501.q: Well in New York I knew a lot of jazz musicians and I knew them very well. I mean that was a part of our world. The thing about the lower Manhattan arts scene in the 1960s was about as close as America ever got to say Montmartre at the turn of the 19th and 20th century, the modernism there. A great…

448.t: Hearing music on 52nd Street; a night at Kelly's Stable with Coleman Hawkins
448.s: Describes the New York club and radio scene and the night he and Denny Strong missed the train and heard Hawkins play Body and Soul.
448.q: Well of course in those days we had 52nd Street, which was this marvelous block between 5th and 6th Avenue, which had, at any given time there was at least four or five different jazz clubs. They’d often change names and management and so forth, but it was great place to hear music. We had Nick’s…

141.t: The 34th Street jazz loft and meeting George Wallington
141.s: He played nightly at the loft, meeting Henry Grimes and Frank Isola; Wallington offered to publish his music.
141.q: I remember that George said he would publish your music, and I was thinking, “Ahh, Tin Pan Alley” and that kind of... I thought it was wonderful. I didn’t realize that we just had to pay $10, and...

143.t: First New York trip, Giants game and Don Byas on 52nd Street
143.s: With the A&T band he visited New York, heard Dizzy's group on 52nd Street, and found Don Byas outplaying an absent Parker.
143.q: The North Carolina A&T band, One of our players, a guy named Stonewall Jackson [Robert ‘Stonewall’ Jackson] , was signed by the Giants, and we came up and played the halftime ceremonies.

527.t: 52nd Street, jam sessions and getting fired from jobs
527.s: Staying late on 52nd Street, sitting in with Dizzy's big band, hearing Bird, Hawkins and Tatum.
527.q: Oh yeah, I went to jam sessions, sure. I used to hang out on 52nd Street. I was working at Radio City Music Hall, and I was supposed to be there at a certain time, but many nights I was late because I was on 52nd Street. So, one night they fired me, so I walked right across the street to the RCA…

328.t: The Carnegie night, Lionel Hampton's band and Bud Powell at Birdland
328.s: First trip to New York: Lionel Hampton's unamplified band, then Birdland with Bud Powell.
328.ch: Carnegie Hall, bebop and the big bands
328.q: Yeah, yeah. It was a really fantastic night. We played. We were good. We were all right. But Lionel Hampton’s band was fantastic. They were . . .

371.t: Arriving in New York with Hot Lips Page and playing boogie-woogie
371.s: Jones joined Page's blues-based band at the Onyx Club, billed as the kid from the West who played boogie-woogie.
371.q: It was 1943. And might have been 1946. Because, I saw Jazz with the Philharmonic in 1946. So, prior to that I had worked on the street for some time. When I first arrived in New York, I worked with the Hot Lips Page Group. We had Buford Oliver playing drums. Karl "Flat Top” Wilson playing bass, and…

224.t: First trip to New York and 52nd Street
224.s: At about 18 he went with his father to New York, visited 52nd Street and first saw Dizzy Gillespie.
224.ch: Boston drummers and a first New York trip
224.q: I would come to New York on weekends when I wasn’t working, before I ever went to join the band. The first time I come to New York, my brother Vin was stationed in Jersey.

135.t: Three Deuces, January 1948, and living in McGhee's Harlem apartment
135.s: Heath describes playing 52nd Street with McGhee's sextet and big band while living with Jimmy in McGhee's 115th Street walk-up, not having moved to New York.
135.q: In New York. In January of ’48 after we came back from Chicago. Erroneously, I hadn’t moved. It’s been reported that I moved to New York. I didn’t move to New York. I came over here to do a gig. We were living in Maggie’s apartment, a five story walk-up over on 115th Street.

372.t: Leaving Thornhill and first night on Fifty-second Street
372.s: Konitz left when the band reached New York, checked into a hotel and went straight to Fifty-second Street.
372.q: I don’t remember that but I remember checking into a hotel and kind of running to Fifty-second Street which wasn’t far away. I think the hotel was in the forties or something like that.

226.t: Arriving in New York: the Onyx Club dump and Harlem crowds
226.s: He was disappointed by the Onyx Club and by arriving at Grand Central, then saw crowds on Lenox Avenue.
226.q: I was disappointed with the club the first day I walked into it. This little greasy looking joint, in the middle of the day, and I said, oh, no. A little bitty bandstand. The clubs we played in Chicago were much nicer clubs and better rooms than – I said, so this is New York, this is 52nd Street,…

104.t: Never going to Harlem, and finding Mary Lou Williams at the Down Beat
104.s: She never went to Harlem or Minton's but finally found Mary Lou at the Down Beat on 52nd Street, where she also met Billy Taylor and John Lewis.
104.ch: Marriage, Chicago and arriving in New York
104.q: . . . go there. At that time you could go anywhere. It wasn’t that you’d be afraid to go somewhere. I would have loved to have been . . . later . . . I didn’t think of how important it would have been to go to somewhere like Minton’s, but as it was, I was trying to ferret out people that I knew…

100.t: First visits to 52nd Street and meeting Nat Lorber
100.s: Wanting to see 52nd Street first, Fay Harrison and her introduction to Nat 'Face' Lorber.
100.q: Like I said in my ten seconds on Ken Burns, most people, when they come to New York for the first time, they want to see the Empire State Building, but I wanted to see 52nd Street. That was the truth. I went down there, because I – it’s not – New York is easy to find your way around, because the…

408.t: Bus trips to New York for Lennie Tristano lessons and 52nd Street
408.s: Summer lessons with Tristano, Romeo's spaghetti, Main Stem records and nights on 52nd Street at age 15.
408.q: me out, that he played the first free, what they call free jazz. I, I like to play expensive jazz, but that’s another story. [MN laughs] Uh, so we’d go to New York from Springfield, Massachusetts, it’s about a three hour bus ride, and then we’d take a subway out to Long Island, I couldn’t tell you…

64.t: Being welcomed in New York: Ram Ramirez and playing with Machito
64.s: He says he was accepted on arrival, recalls Ram Ramirez and Judy Holiday's Village scene, and his first work with Machito's band at a Latin club.
64.ch: New York scene and bebop community
64.q: I was accepted right away, as were most people who first came. When I first came to New York, I came around the same time as Errol Garner, and Pipe Jones, and we all were just welcomed with open arms to 52nd Street. There were a lot of musicians who lived here, who were not for a variety of reasons…

376.t: First trip to America: Miami and Bill Gottlieb
376.s: On a trip with his uncle he sat in at a Miami restaurant, met photographer Bill Gottlieb, and was taken to 52nd Street.
376.ch: Bebop and the first American trip
376.q: And as it was, I had made… I came to the States in ’47 with my uncle, and I met Hank Jones and those guys at 52nd Street. That was the Three Deuces. And every week there was an all-star group but with the same guys. One week was J.J. Johnson, the leader. One week was Howard McGee, a fine trumpet…

219.t: Visiting 52nd Street while his brother was at NYU
219.s: Wein drove to New York to hear Tatum, Hawkins, Basie and others on 52nd Street.
219.q: My brother went to several colleges. (chuckles) He didn't last too long at any of them because he didn't want it … he knew he was going in the Army and so he didn't care. But he did spend a few months at NYU.

381.t: The Rhythm Club, Kaiser Marshall and other musicians from Florida
381.s: He visited the Rhythm Club and met Kaiser Marshall, Cedric Wallace and Cookie Mason.
381.q: Yeah, I first met Cozy Cole -- up there and my eyes popped wide open; I didn't know about the Rhythm Club yet. See, this was about my third night in town. Well, the next day, I heard that -- that night, I heard them talking about the Rhythm Club. Well, I had heard the guys down in Miami talk about…

235.t: Arriving in New York and living over Minton's Playhouse
235.s: He describes coming by bus, staying at the hotel by Minton's, and hearing Lester Young, Don Byas, Monk, Kenny Clarke and others, with Teddy Hill as owner.
235.q: Yeah. It was my first trip to New York and of course Minton's Playhouse was the place, you know what I mean. Everybody was there...

239.t: First weeks in New York in 1944: the Onyx, 52nd Street and a big city
239.s: Jones describes arriving in New York, hearing Tatum, Gillespie, Hawkins, Byas and Monk, sightseeing, and deciding never to live in Chicago again.
239.q: Oh, I have something funny to tell you about that. As soon as we got to New York and got established where we were going to stay, or live, and in those days New York was so beautiful, I knew then I was never going to go back to Chicago. Just to see my people and my father and whatever, but I wasn't…

112.t: Charley Johnson precedes him to New York; the Big Apple
112.s: Johnson went to Baron's before Wooding; Wooding does not recall New York being called the Big Apple except for a club.
112.q: Because I know there was a place there in New York that we used to all frequent, called the "Big Apple", right across there from Smalls. But I don't remember that statement, that we were in the "Big Apple".
